claims.text: High configurational entropy contributes to the structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic multimetal nanoparticles.
Kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion induced by lattice distortion govern nanoparticle stability.
Atomic-size mismatches produce significant local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions hinder atomic rearrangement and phase separation at lower temperatures.
Reducing lattice distortion lowers the kinetic barrier to atomic rearrangement.
Lower kinetic barriers promote local ordering and eventual phase separation at elevated temperatures.
The initial nanoparticles are single-phase, disordered solid solutions with significant lattice strain.
Substitution with chemically similar elements having closer atomic radii will reduce lattice distortion while preserving a near-equiatomic composition.
Lattice distortions impose kinetic barriers to elemental diffusion.
Diffusion barriers control the onset of local ordering and phase segregation.
Significant lattice distortions kinetically trap the baseline nanoparticles in a disordered solid-solution state even at elevated temperatures.
Reduced lattice distortion enhances atomic mobility.
Enhanced atomic mobility facilitates local ordering and phase separation as temperature approaches thermoelectric operating conditions.
Modified nanoparticles with reduced lattice distortion will show an earlier onset of local ordering and phase segregation above approximately 1000 K than the baseline nanoparticles.
Baseline nanoparticles will largely retain their metastable solid-solution character throughout 473–1923 K.
Oxidizing atmospheres or extremely long thermal dwell times may introduce stability behavior not captured by the proposed lattice-distortion model.
